doc.title: JJ Johnson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Band uniforms and whether Carter's band was integrated
summary: Uniforms were expected; Johnson recalls no white members, contradicting a dissertation Baker cites.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: I’m trying to remember the picture that you are talking about. Did you all wear uniforms with that band?
No, just as a part of your normal . . .
Oh, the photograph that you have?
Uh huh. As a part of your normal appearance where . . .
Is the question did Benny Carter’s band wear band uniforms?
Did you all wear uniforms? I know a lot of the bands did.
Oh, certainly. I’m sure we did. I’m sure we did.
Because some of those were very, very stylish, wonderful . . .
Oh, yeah. Most bands of importance and even not of importance had [them]. It was the order of the day to have band uniforms. Yes. Yes. It was expected. It was very prevalent.
That was an integrated band, from what I understand. [Johnson and David Baker look surprised.] No, that was not an integrated band?
Okay. I'm looking at Louis's [Louis G. Bourgois III] dissertation here, and he talked about the fact that [it] was an integrated band and [that] there were some problems as a result of that.
On the picture it was not.
I don’t recall . . . you mean Benny’s band?

I don’t recall there being any white members of Benny’s band. That’s not to say that Benny’s band never included a white musician, but while I was there, there was never a white musician. That I can say with some accuracy. During the two or three year stint with Benny that I was there, it was not an integrated band. We'll have to speak to Bourgois about that. [The Bakers laugh]
